in_text_mentions: A 45-year-old woman was referred to our breast clinic due to slow growing bilateral breast enlargement since 2 years priorly, with more growth on the left, causing significant asymmetry (Figure 1). In clinical examination, both breasts were enlarged with multiple lumps which were soft and mobile upon palpation. The overlying skin was thickened and erythematous on the left side. Soft lumps were also palpable in both axillae. The patient did not have any systemic disease, was premenopausal, had not received any hormonal therapy, and had no family history of breast cancer.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Panel (a) shows the characteristic anastomosing groups of spindle cells within the stroma of the breast, which fits the diagnosis of Pseudoangiomatous Stromal Hyperplasia as described in the caption and article. b: Panel (b) displays the classic pseudoangiomatous pattern characterized by stromal spindle cells lining slit-like spaces, consistent with the diagnosis of Pseudoangiomatous Stromal Hyperplasia.

panels.figure_caption: (a) Anastomosing groups of spindle cells in the stroma. Normal breast epithelium top left. (b) Stromal spindle cells which appear to be lining slit-like spaces devoid of red blood cells.
in_text_mentions: Fine needle aspiration cytology results were equivocal showing cohesive cells with focal mild nuclear atypia and numerous bare nuclei. Core biopsy was done that showed the presence of spindle cells in the fibrous tissue in a pseudoangiomatous pattern which fitted the diagnosis of PASH. This was the same finding on the final histopathology after excision (Figure 3). Immunohistochemistry was positive for CD34 and Vimentin while Factor VIII, cytokeratin, progesterone, and oestrogen receptors were negative.

plate_findings.evidence: T2-weighted imaging showed high-signal slit-like spaces (long arrows).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Panel A shows high-signal slit-like spaces on T2-weighted MRI, a characteristic finding of Pseudoangiomatous Stromal Hyperplasia. B: Panel B shows low signal on T1-weighted MRI, consistent with the imaging findings described for Pseudoangiomatous Stromal Hyperplasia. C: Panel C displays a dynamic enhancement curve showing an ascending pattern, which is mentioned in the context of the masses in this case of PAH. D: Panel D shows low signal on fat suppression imaging, a finding consistent with the diagnosis of Pseudoangiomatous Stromal Hyperplasia. E: Panel E shows multiple oval-shaped masses with clear boundaries, an imaging manifestation described in the context of Pseudoangiomatous Stromal Hyperplasia. F: Panel F shows diffusion-weighted imaging with mild diffusion restriction, reported as a finding in the enhanced masses associated with PAH.
panels.attribution_text: Lian et al. Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia causing bilateral galactomastia with short-term recurrence after surgery: a case report.. The Journal of international medical research 2024. doi:10.1177/03000605241293684. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Magnetic resonance imaging findings of pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia. (a) T2-weighted imaging showed high-signal slit-like spaces (long arrows). (b) T1-weighted imaging showed low-signal areas, and (d) T1-weighted fat suppression imaging also demonstrated low signals. (e) These slit-like spaces (long arrows) showed no enhancement, while multiple oval-shaped masses (short arrows) with clear boundaries were observed. (c) The dynamic enhancement curve was ascending. (f) Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed mild diffusion restriction within the enhanced masses.
in_text_mentions: Mammography indicated diffuse enlargement of both breasts without visible calcifications and appeared to show multiple masses (Figure 2). Magnetic resonance imaging revealed bilateral breast enlargement with multiple slit-like spaces (Figure 3) exhibiting low signals on T1-weighted images and high signals on T2-weighted images. These spaces showed no enhancement. Multiple oval-shaped masses with clear boundaries were observed within the lesions, with an ascending dynamic enhancement curve. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated mild diffusion restriction in the enhanced masses.

Six months previously, she visited our hospital for further diagnosis and treatment because of movement limitations and respiratory difficulties. Physical examination revealed asymmetrical bilateral gigantomastia, with the left breast extending to the umbilical level and the right breast positioned approximately two finger breadths above the umbilical level (Figure 1(a)). The patient underwent bilateral subcutaneous mastectomy for excision of bilateral axillary ectopic breast tissue under general anesthesia. Pathology revealed PASH with complete excision (Figure 2). Stains for CD34, CD31, and factor VIII were not conducted as the mass had benign characteristics both on imaging and pathology assessment. At a follow-up two weeks later, the patient showed no evidence of recurrence, infection, or wound breakdown.

The ducts are present in a dense hyalinized stroma which shows features of pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (Figures 2–4).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A is a diagnostic mammogram showing a focal asymmetry in the left breast, consistent with the diagnosis of Pseudoangiomatous Stromal Hyperplasia, supported by the article title and context. B: Panel B is a post-biopsy mammogram of the left breast showing a marker clip within the mass. The context identifies this mass as related to Pseudoangiomatous Stromal Hyperplasia. C: Panel C is a diagnostic ultrasound of the left breast showing a hypoechoic, irregular mass with angular margins, which corresponds to the clinical description of the mass affected by Pseudoangiomatous Stromal Hyperplasia.

panels.figure_caption: Imaging Findings of Pseudoangiomatous Stromal Hyperplasia (A) A diagnostic mammogram of left breast shows a subareolar focal asymmetry at the site of palpable marker (yellow triangle). (B) A post-biopsy mammogram of left breast demonstrates a ribbon biopsy marker clip within the biopsied mass (red circle), in the subareolar region. (C) A diagnostic ultrasound of left breast shows a hypoechoic irregular mass with angular margins (blue circle) with no internal vascularity, measuring 9 millimeters in the subareolar 12 o’clock region.
in_text_mentions: The ultrasound imaging for this patient on his second presentation showed a hypoechoic, irregular mass, with angular margins and without internal vascularity. The mass measured 9 mm in the subareolar 12 o'clock region, consistent with nodular-type gynecomastia (Figure 3).
